faq.a: Yes; early malaria may present with malaise and mild fever or even afebrile, especially in semi‑immune adults.
faq.q: Can malaise be a sign of malaria without fever?

faq.a: Start empiric antimalarial therapy if microscopy is unavailable, and repeat RDT or obtain microscopy when possible.
faq.q: What is the first step if malaria RDT is negative but suspicion is high?

faq.a: HIV leads to persistent immune activation, anemia, and opportunistic infections, all contributing to a feeling of unwellness.

exam: What bedside findings would make you prioritize malaria testing in a patient with malaise? — Look for recent travel to endemic area, intermittent fever, chills, and splenomegaly.
A patient with malaise has a normal temperature but is hypotensive. What is your next step? — Treat as possible sepsis: obtain blood cultures, give empiric antibiotics, and start fluid resuscitation.
How does anemia present differently from infection as a cause of malaise? — Anemia shows pallor, tachycardia, low hemoglobin; infection often adds fever, leukocytosis, and localized signs.
Why might a malaria RDT be falsely negative, and how do you manage it? — Low parasite density or HRP2 gene deletion; repeat test or use microscopy, consider empiric therapy if clinical picture fits.

In a resource‑limited setting, which single investigation gives the most information for a patient with malaise, fever, and weight loss? — Full blood count, because it screens for anemia, leukocytosis, and thrombocytopenia, guiding further work‑up.
What red‑flag symptom in a patient with chronic malaise suggests adrenal insufficiency? — Persistent hypotension with hyperpigmentation and hyponatremia.

How would you differentiate between depression‑related fatigue and systemic malaise? — Depression lacks fever, weight loss, and abnormal labs; systemic malaise shows objective signs of infection or organ dysfunction.

Why is it important to give supportive care before a definitive diagnosis in patients with severe malaise? — Early fluid, nutrition, and symptom control prevent deterioration while investigations are pending.
ai.title: Malaise in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Malaise is a nonspecific feeling of discomfort, fatigue, or illness. It is a common presenting symptom in low‑resource settings and often signals underlying infection, metabolic disturbance, or chronic disease.

b: Often accompanies fever, weight loss, or pain
May be the sole symptom in early HIV, TB, or malaria
sections.p: Malaise is a subjective sense of being unwell without a specific focal complaint. It prompts a systematic search for reversible causes, especially infections and metabolic derangements common in East Africa.

b: Infection: malaria, TB, HIV, bacterial sepsis
Metabolic: anemia, electrolyte imbalance, renal failure
Chronic disease: malignancy, heart failure, sickle‑cell crisis
sections.p: Approach malaise by categorising possible aetiologies: infectious, inflammatory, metabolic, haematologic, endocrine, and psychosocial. Use bedside clues to narrow the list.

b: Identify red flags: high fever, hypotension, altered mental status, severe weight loss
Prioritise investigations that are available locally
sections.p: Malaise can be the first sign of life‑threatening disease. Prompt identification of red‑flag features and targeted investigations guide early treatment, improving outcomes in low‑resource hospitals.

t.b: Detect anemia, leukocytosis or leukopenia; guides infection vs haematologic cause
Confirms Plasmodium infection when fever present; negative RDT + high suspicion → microscopy if possible
Screen for HIV infection, a common cause of chronic malaise
Detects protein, glucose, or infection; useful when renal disease suspected
Looks for TB, pneumonia, or cardiac enlargement

Broad‑spectrum antibiotics for suspected sepsis after cultures
Correct electrolyte or glucose abnormalities promptly
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause; provide supportive care while awaiting results.

Depression: low mood with anhedonia, not usually accompanied by fever
sections.p: Malaise is frequently mistaken for simple fatigue or depression, but it often signals systemic disease.
